Your child has dropped. Dead weight. Cars waiting. People staring.
This isn't defiance. This isn't bad parenting. This is a nervous system speaking the only language it knows right now. Here are 9 evidence-based materials that address the why — and give you the what-now.

Act I — Understanding
This Is a Wiring Difference. Not a Behaviour Choice.
What's Happening Neurologically
Proprioceptive Processing Deficit — Floor dropping often occurs when the proprioceptive system under-registers body-position input. The child seeks deep pressure (floor contact = full-body compression) to self-regulate.
Prefrontal Cortex Dysregulation — Under high demand or sensory load, the executive function centre cannot modulate the amygdala's threat-detection response. The child's nervous system enters shutdown/escape mode.
Transition Dysregulation — Abrupt transitions disrupt the brain's predictive coding mechanisms. Without advance warning, the brain has no framework for "what comes next" — triggering a collapse response.
What This Means for Your Child
🧠 Your child's nervous system craves deep pressure. The floor is the largest pressure source available. The body drops to get the input it needs.
⚡ When overwhelmed, your child cannot choose their response. The thinking brain goes offline. The survival brain takes over. Dropping is the body's emergency brake.
🔮 Surprises trigger shutdown. When your child doesn't know what's coming next, the brain treats uncertainty as a threat — and collapse is the escape response.

This is NOT wilful defiance. Functional MRI research shows atypical sensory gating in autistic children — the nervous system literally processes sensory input differently. These are neurological facts, not excuses.
Act I — Developmental Context
Your Child Is Here. Here Is Where We're Heading.
In typically developing children, floor dropping naturally decreases as verbal communication and self-regulation skills emerge (ages 3–5). In children with ASD, sensory processing differences, or communication delays, floor dropping can persist and entrench if the underlying function is not addressed. The good news: neural plasticity is highest in the early intervention window.
Age 1–2
Floor dropping begins as typical protest behaviour
Age 2–4 ⚠️
Peak Challenge Zone — Limited verbal expression, high sensory sensitivity, increasing demands
Age 4–7 ✅
Intervention Window — Neural plasticity highest; behavioural patterns most responsive to structured intervention
Age 7–10
Consolidation phase — replacement behaviours becoming habitual
Age 10–12+
Community navigation readiness — independent regulation strategies

WHO Milestone Alignment: The WHO Care for Child Development Package identifies behavioural self-regulation as a Developmental Readiness Indicator. Floor dropping that continues beyond age 5 warrants structured intervention. Floor dropping commonly co-occurs with: Sensory Processing Disorder · Transition Intolerance · Limited Verbal Communication · Anxiety · Proprioceptive Seeking.

Act II — The Knowledge Transfer
Floor Dropping — Functional Behavioural Support Protocol
"The Ground Plan" — 9 tools to address why your child drops and what to do about it. Floor Dropping Behaviour is a pattern where a child suddenly collapses to the ground, becoming limp or resistant, typically in public settings or during transitions. Unlike tantrums, floor dropping is primarily a motor response — often serving sensory, escape, communication, or regulation functions. Effective support addresses the underlying function, not just the behaviour.
🎯 Age Range
2–12 years across all settings
🏠 Settings
Home · Community · Stores · Parking Lots · Schools
👩‍⚕️ Disciplines
OT · ABA/BCBA · SLP (if communication function)
⏱ Duration
Daily application across all environments

Act II — Disciplines
Five Disciplines. One Converged Strategy. Maximum Impact.
Occupational Therapist (OT)
Primary Lead: Sensory Materials
Designs weighted vest protocol, proprioceptive kit, noise-cancelling headphone selection. Conducts Sensory Profile 2 to identify sensory-seeking patterns driving floor dropping. Prescribes 5–10% body weight for vest.
Behaviour Analyst (ABA/BCBA)
Primary Lead: Functional Intervention
Conducts Functional Behaviour Assessment (FBA). Designs the break card system, motivator bag reinforcement schedule, ABC data collection. Implements function-matched replacement behaviours.
Speech-Language Pathologist (SLP)
Supporting Role: Communication Function
When floor dropping primarily communicates "I need a break," SLP designs Functional Communication Training (FCT) and AAC integration into the break card system.
Special Educator (SpEd)
Supporting Role: Predictability Systems
Designs visual schedules, first-then boards, social stories for school and community settings. Creates individualised transition protocols.
NeuroDevelopmental Paediatrician
Oversight: Medical Rule-Out
Rules out underlying medical factors (hypotonia, vestibular disorders, pain) before behavioural intervention begins. Provides diagnostic clarity for GPT-OS® profiling.

Consortium Note: Floor dropping may be 40% sensory (OT), 30% behavioural (ABA), 20% communication (SLP), 10% adaptive (SpEd) — for your child specifically. GPT-OS® FusionModule™ coordinates all inputs into a single plan.
Act II — Targets
Floor Dropping Serves 4 Functions. These Materials Address All of Them.

Important: Most children's floor dropping serves multiple functions simultaneously. A Functional Behaviour Assessment (FBA) by a BCBA identifies the primary function for YOUR child. Until then, these 9 materials cover all likely functions.
Material 1 of 9
Weighted Compression Vest
Meeting pressure needs while staying upright
The Science
Many children who floor drop are proprioceptive seekers — their nervous system craves deep pressure input. The floor provides full-body compression. A weighted vest delivers the same proprioceptive input continuously while the child remains upright.
Research shows 5–10% of body weight, worn for structured intervals, can significantly reduce sensory-seeking behaviours and improve behavioural regulation.
What · Where · When · How
  • WHAT: Vest containing small weights (typically 200g–600g); compression vests provide similar calming input without weight
  • WHERE: Community outings, stores, school transitions, wherever floor dropping peaks
  • WHEN: 20–30 minutes before and during challenging activities; NOT worn all day
  • HOW: OT prescribes exact weight (5–10% body weight). Put on 5 minutes before the outing with a visual cue
DIY Option (₹0): A snug-fitting compression shirt provides similar input at zero cost. Small fabric pouches with rice sewn into vest pockets. Always consult your OT for correct weight protocol.

⚠️ Safety Note: Never exceed 10% body weight. Remove if child shows discomfort. Maximum wearing intervals: 20 minutes on / 20 minutes off. Not for use during sleep. Price Range: ₹1,500 – ₹4,000
Material 2 of 9
Visual Schedule / First-Then Board
Predictability reduces transition meltdowns
The Science
Unpredictable transitions disrupt the brain's predictive coding systems. When a child doesn't know what comes after the current activity, the brain registers uncertainty as a threat — triggering the escape response (floor dropping). Visual schedules make time and sequence concrete and visible.
"First store, then playground" — spoken words are processed and forgotten in seconds. A visual board stays accessible, revisable, and empowering.
What · Where · When · How
  • WHAT: Laminated board showing TWO items: current demand + upcoming preferred activity. Or a strip showing 3–5 activities in sequence
  • WHERE: Home morning routine, car trips, store entrances — everywhere
  • WHEN: Show and review BEFORE entering the challenging setting. Review again if you see pre-drop warning signs
  • HOW: Show board → point to each image → say it aloud → "First [activity], THEN [reward]." When task complete, remove/flip the first card
DIY Option (₹50–100): Print photos of your actual home, store, park, school. Laminate with contact paper. Attach velcro strips. Free PECS symbols at boardmakeronline.com.

⚠️ Safety Note: Ensure the "THEN" activity actually happens. Breaking the promise destroys the board's credibility and worsens behavioural trust. Price Range: ₹200 – ₹800
Material 3 of 9
Break Card / Communication Support
An acceptable way to say "I need to stop"
The Science
For many children, floor dropping IS communication. It's how they say "no," "I need a break," "this is too much" — when words aren't accessible. Functional Communication Training (FCT) gives the child an acceptable channel for the same message.
The key: the break card must WORK. When the child uses it, a real break must follow. This teaches that communication is more powerful than collapse.
How to Introduce (4 Steps)
  1. Introduce: "When you need a break, hand me this card"
  1. Practice at home: Give card → parent says "great asking!" → 2-minute break
  1. Community: Same protocol, honoured consistently
  1. Fade: Over weeks, expand tolerance before card earns break
What: Laminated "BREAK" card with visual symbol, worn on lanyard or clipped to shirt — always on their person, not in a bag.
DIY Option (₹30–50): Print and laminate. Attach to a lanyard. Use a photo of something calming on the back.

⚠️ NEVER deny the break after the card is used. If you can't honour it, don't introduce the system. Inconsistency accelerates floor dropping. Classified Level I Evidence-Based Practice by NCAEP 2020. Price Range: ₹100 – ₹500
Material 4 of 9
Proprioceptive Activity Kit
Regulating tools that travel with you
The Science
When floor dropping serves a sensory or regulatory function, proactive proprioceptive input prevents the dysregulation cascade before collapse occurs. This kit provides on-the-go organising input that keeps the nervous system regulated through challenging environments.
The key is PROACTIVE use: offer kit tools before you see warning signs, not after the drop.
Kit Contents + How to Use
  • Resistance band or theraband loop
  • Stress ball / squeeze toy
  • Chewy tube or chewelry
  • Small weighted palm item
WHEN: Proactively at outing start + during shopping. If you see early warning signs → offer kit immediately.
DIY Option (₹50–150): Resistance band: cut a 30cm loop from theraband (₹80/roll). Squeeze ball: balloon filled with flour or rice (₹5). Total DIY kit: under ₹150.

⚠️ Early Warning Signs — Act Now: Pacing slowing · Eyes going glassy · Starting to sit on floor · Hands going to ears · Visible tension building → THIS is when you offer the kit, not after the drop. Price Range: ₹400 – ₹1,200
Material 5 of 9
FREE Helpline: 9100 181 181
Noise-Cancelling Headphones
Reducing the overwhelm that leads to collapse
The Science
Floor dropping in stores, malls, and crowds often occurs because auditory overload pushes the child past their regulatory threshold. Fluorescent light hum, music, crowd noise, cart sounds, announcements — collectively these can create a neurological wall that collapses the child's regulation capacity.
Noise-cancelling headphones reduce auditory input to a manageable level. For some children, the headphones provide a predictability "bubble" — "when I wear these, the world is manageable."
Gradual Introduction (4 Steps)
  1. Home desensitisation: Wear headphones for 5 mins during comfortable home activity
  1. Quiet community: Park, low-traffic shop
  1. Medium-noise environment: Small supermarket
  1. Full challenging environment: Busy mall or market
Routine: "Headphones on = we're going in" — put on BEFORE entering, not after distress begins.
DIY Option (₹200–400): Children's ear defenders (tool stores) provide excellent passive noise reduction. Loop earplugs (less conspicuous): ₹400–800.

⚠️ Safety Note — Outdoors: In parking lots and near traffic: maintain hand or wrist contact. Headphones may reduce traffic sound awareness. Wrist Link (Material 7) + headphones = safest combination for outdoor environments. Price Range: ₹1,000 – ₹5,000
Material 6 of 9
Motivator Bag with Reinforcement Items
Changing the equation from escape to reward
The Science
When floor dropping is escape-maintained — the child drops to avoid demands and the behaviour succeeds (demands stop) — motivation becomes the central intervention. A motivator bag makes staying upright more valuable than escaping.
ABA Principle: Behaviour that is reinforced increases. Make cooperation the behaviour that earns the best reinforcers.
Before · During · After Protocol
  • BEFORE entering: Show bag, name what's inside, establish contingency
  • DURING (longer outings): Intermittent access with token economy
  • AFTER: Deliver reinforcer within 30 seconds of completing the task
Reinforcement Menu Ideas: Small puzzle piece · Favourite song on phone · 3 minutes of preferred video · Special sticker · Favourite snack · Specific toy · Token toward larger reward
DIY Option (₹0–100): Any distinctive bag (colour not used otherwise) filled with items your child already loves. The bag and its scarcity are the intervention.

⚠️ Never show the bag if you won't actually deliver the reward. Promise kept = trust built = behaviour improves. Preference assessment: what does your child love MOST that isn't available routinely? Restrict access to bag items outside outings. Price Range: ₹300 – ₹1,000
Material 7 of 9
Wrist Link / Safety Harness
Maintaining safety when floor drops happen

⚠️ Non-Negotiable Safety Frame: In parking lots with moving vehicles, busy streets, crowded markets, and anywhere a sudden floor drop creates a safety emergency — physical connection is not optional. Address the behaviour AND maintain safety simultaneously.
Why It Works
A wrist link provides: (1) Physical safety — prevents the child from becoming unreachable during a drop. (2) Proprioceptive regulation — the constant gentle pressure of the link provides ongoing body-position awareness. (3) Visual cue — "we stay together" is communicated through the link, reducing the impulse to drop as an escape.
For some children, the physical connection itself is regulating — parental proximity through proprioceptive input.
How to Introduce
Introduce at home first ("wrist buddy for our adventures"). Never use as punishment. Always paired with positive framing: "this keeps you safe so we can go to exciting places."
Non-negotiable settings: Parking lots · Traffic-adjacent areas · Crowded markets/festivals · Train stations · Anywhere floor drop = danger
People may stare. Some may comment. You have permission to say: "My child has a developmental difference and this is their safety device." You owe no further explanation. Your child's safety matters more than a stranger's opinion.
DIY Note: Wrist links are safety devices, NOT restraints. Never drag a child by the link. Hold gentle steady pressure and wait. Price Range: ₹300 – ₹1,200
Material 8 of 9
Transition Timer / Warning System
Making transitions predictable and visible
Many floor drops occur in the 30-second window of a sudden transition. "We're leaving NOW" — with no advance warning — triggers the nervous system's threat-detection response. Visual timers make abstract time CONCRETE. The child can see the red section shrinking. Surprise is eliminated.
1
⏱ 5-Minute Warning
Show timer, point to red section. "Five more minutes, then we put on shoes."
2
⏱ 2-Minute Warning
"Two more minutes. Getting close." Offer prep activity: "Want to hold the shopping list?"
3
⏱ 1-Minute Warning
"One more minute. Timer almost done." Start transition preparation: get coat, put on shoes.
4
✅ Transition
Timer ends (auditory cue). "All done! Time to go." Show First-Then board. Transition occurs.

⚠️ Once the timer is set, honour it. DO NOT extend time ("just 5 more minutes"). This destroys the predictability value and teaches that protests work. DIY Option (₹0): Phone timer + paper 5-2-1 warning cards. Sand timers (hourglass) are often more engaging for young children. Price Range: ₹500 – ₹2,000
Material 9 of 9
Social Stories
Teaching what to expect and what to do instead
The Science
Social stories (Gray, 1991) prepare the child cognitively for what will happen, how they might feel, and what they can DO. Cognitive preparation reduces the uncertainty that triggers floor dropping. The brain with a prepared script is less likely to go into emergency mode.
Read at HOME before the outing — consistently, multiple times. Read the relevant social story the morning of the outing AND in the car before entering.
How to Write Your Story (4 Steps)
  1. Write about SPECIFIC locations (your actual store, the actual parking lot)
  1. Include photos of the actual places when possible
  1. Include all 4 narrative types: descriptive (what is) · perspective (how I feel) · directive (what I do) · affirmative (why it matters)
  1. Read 3–5 times per week, not just before challenging outings
DIY Option (₹0): Write on paper, add drawn or printed images. Google Slides = free digital social stories. Free templates: carolgraysocialstories.com framework.
"When I go to the grocery store with Amma, sometimes I feel tired or overwhelmed. My body might want to sit on the floor. When I feel like this, I can use my break card. Amma will give me a short break. After our shopping, we go to [preferred place]. I am a good helper."
Sample Social Story Starter — adapt with your child's name, your actual store, and your child's preferred place. Price Range: ₹200 – ₹600 | NCAEP 2020 classified Evidence-Based Practice.
Act III — How To Use
Step 1: Readiness Check — Is Today a Go?
The best outing is one that starts right. Observe these indicators before leaving home. Not every outing needs to happen today — strategic postponement is not avoidance, it's setting up success. Repeated failures entrench the pattern. Repeated successes build new neural pathways.
🟢 GO — All Conditions Met
  • Child slept well (≥8 hours for age)
  • Child has eaten (not hungry)
  • No illness indicators
  • Current sensory state: regulated
  • Time window: not end-of-day fatigue
  • Materials packed: vest / headphones / break card / kit / motivator bag
🟡 MODIFY — Some Flags Present
  • Child is tired but manageable
  • Minor illness symptoms
  • Outing is necessary
Action: Shorten outing by 40%. Double the proactive regulation tools. Go with clear exit strategy.
🔴 POSTPONE — High-Risk Indicators
  • Child has already had one dysregulation episode today
  • Illness confirmed
  • Sleep deprivation (child or caregiver)
  • Already in sensory overload
Action: Postpone non-essential outings. If essential: use all 9 materials, plan 15-minute maximum, have car as immediate exit.
Act III — Step 2
The Invitation — How to Begin
Every protocol begins with an invitation. Not a command. The pre-outing sequence takes 5–10 minutes total. Do not rush this — it is therapy.
1
5 Minutes Before Leaving
Review First-Then Board: "First [outing], then [preferred activity]. Show me!" Check all materials: vest ON · headphones ready · break card clipped · kit in bag · motivator bag visible. Read social story if not done this morning.
2
At the Door
"Today we're going to [store]. You have your break card [point]. If it gets too loud, here are your headphones [show]. When we finish, we get [specific motivator]. Ready?"
3
In the Car
Set transition timer for travel time. Visual schedule review if possible. Calming preferred music or audiobook (headphones if beneficial).
4
At the Destination Entrance
"We're here! Break card is ready. Timer starts now." 5-minute warning routine begins from entry.
✅ Acceptance Cues (child is ready)
  • Body oriented toward you
  • Eye contact or orientation
  • No protest vocalisations
  • Hands available (not protecting ears)
  • Walking pace normal
⚠️ Resistance Cues (modify approach)
  • Body turning away
  • Hands to ears
  • Feet slowing
  • Vocalisation of distress
  • Seeking floor contact
→ Return to car, use proprioceptive kit, reassess.
Act III — Step 3
The Engagement — During the Outing
What you do during the outing determines whether it becomes a pattern. Monitor your child's regulation state every 5 minutes. Proactive intervention prevents drops — reactive intervention stops them from escalating.
Every 5 Minutes — Observe
Regulated ✓ | Building tension ⚠️ | Pre-drop state 🔴
Pre-drop detected → Offer: proprioceptive kit first · break card opportunity · reduce pace/demands
When Warning Signs Appear
"I can see you might need a break. Do you want to use your card?" Offer break card, point to it, wait 5 seconds. If child uses card → honour break immediately (2 minutes, proprioceptive input). If child doesn't use card → still provide brief regulation break: wall push-ups, squeeze ball, quiet seating.
If Floor Drop Occurs — 7-Step Response
  1. Safety first — wrist link prevents dangerous separation
  1. Stay calm — no raised voice, no commands
  1. Minimal language — "I can see you need a break. I'm here."
  1. Wait — proprioceptive tools offered but not forced
  1. Avoid power struggle — floor dropping escalates when physically confronted
  1. Recovery — once child begins to regulate, offer break card use (post-hoc practice)
  1. Brief exit — outing shortened for this session, celebrated for any progress

Data Capture — Right Now: Quick 60-second tracking: Did floor drop occur? (Y/N) · Setting (store/parking lot/other) · Which materials used · Duration of outing before drop / total outing duration · Apparent trigger (transition/demand/sensory/unknown). Data collection is non-negotiable in ABA — ABC data drives functional hypothesis and plan adaptation.
Act III — Step 4
The Cool-Down — Closing the Outing
No outing ends abruptly. The close is part of the therapy. A structured, celebratory close reinforces the child's effort, delivers the promised reinforcer, and builds positive associations with future outings.
5-Min Warning
"Five more minutes, then we finish. First-then board: [store done, then park/home/reward]."
2-Min Warning
"Two more minutes. Almost done! You're doing so well."
Outing End
"All done! Time to go. You used your [break card / vest / headphones] today — amazing work."
Motivator Delivery
Within 30 seconds of outing completion: "Remember what was in the bag? YOU EARNED IT." Immediate, enthusiastic, specific.
Car Cool-Down
Preferred music or audiobook. Remove vest if wearing. Offer water. Proprioceptive input if needed. Calm, undemanding conversation.
"We did it. [X minutes] in the store. You used your break card TWICE today. That was incredible."

Parent Self-Care Reminder: You carried a lot today. Managing floor dropping in public is exhausting. Your regulation matters too. Take your own breath.
Act III — Step 5
Adapt — Personalise Your Plan
Data-driven personalisation. Because no two children are identical. Use your session data to identify the primary function and adjust your protocol accordingly.
1
🏋️ Sensory Seeking
Increase: Weighted vest wearing time (consult OT) · Pre-outing proprioceptive loading (10 min before) · Floor time at home as scheduled acceptable activity
Reduce: Demand level during highest sensory challenge periods
2
🚪 Escape/Avoidance
Increase: Motivator bag value · First-then board visibility · Token economy density
Reduce: Outing duration (success at 10 minutes > failure at 30 minutes) · Demand density
3
💬 Communication
Increase: Break card practice frequency (5x/day at home) · AAC integration (SLP consult)
Reduce: Time between communication opportunities
4
🔊 Sensory Overload
Increase: Headphone use · Pre-outing sensory diet · Outing timing (quiet hours)
Reduce: Outing frequency until baseline tolerance builds
📉 Easier (Regression / Bad Days)
  • Shorten outing by 50%
  • Increase motivator quality
  • Double proactive proprioceptive input
  • Start at quieter, less challenging environment
📈 Harder (Progress Days)
  • Extend outing by 10–15%
  • Gradually reduce vest wearing time
  • Fade timer warnings (5-2-1 → 2-1 → 1)
  • New, slightly more challenging environment

For personalised adaptation — a BCBA or OT at Pinnacle can conduct a Functional Behaviour Assessment (FBA) and design a precisely matched intervention plan. Call: 9100 181 181 | pinnacleblooms.org
Act IV — The Progress Arc
Weeks 1–2: What Real Progress Looks Like
You are in the early phase. The pattern is still strong. Your consistency is fighting an entrenched behaviour. Every consistent session is a deposit into the neural change account. Week 1–2 is the hardest — and the most important.
✅ What You MAY See (Success Indicators)
  • Floor drops still occurring BUT shorter duration before recovery
  • Child uses break card at least once with prompting
  • Vest accepted without protest (even if not yet effective)
  • Outing completed even if imperfectly
  • Post-drop recovery time decreasing
⏳ What You WON'T See Yet (And That's Normal)
  • Complete elimination of floor dropping
  • Independent break card use without prompting
  • Long outings completed without incident
  • Generalisation to new environments
If your child tolerates the weighted vest for 10 minutes longer than last week — that IS progress. If they looked at the break card even once — that IS the neural pathway beginning.
Act IV — Progress Arc
Weeks 3–4: Neural Pathways Are Forming
What you're seeing is the beginning of synaptic strengthening. The child's brain is learning: "Break card → break happens → this works." This is neuroplasticity in real time. The new pathway is competing with the old (floor drop) pathway. Consistency now is critical.
40%
Consolidation Phase
Progress along the intervention arc by Weeks 3–4
50%
Faster Recovery
Typical reduction in post-drop recovery time (from 10–15 min to 2–3 min)
1/3
Independent Card Use
Children begin reaching for break card independently at least once per outing
Child reaches for break card independently
At least once per outing — even partial, even with one prompt
Floor drops limited to higher-trigger scenarios
Specific stores, longer outings — not every outing
Pre-drop warning signs more predictable
You can see it coming now — this is YOUR skill developing
Vest put-on routine established without resistance
The regulation tool is becoming part of the "going out" ritual

When to Increase Intensity: If child uses break card consistently → start extending outing duration by 15%. If floor drops are limited to 1–2 specific triggers → now is the time for targeted FBA.
Act IV — Progress Arc
Weeks 5–8: Independence Beginning to Emerge
The replacement behaviour (break card / regulation tools) is becoming more efficient than the floor drop at achieving the child's goal. From the nervous system's perspective: communication and regulation tools are out-competing behavioural collapse. This is the emergence phase.
Independent break card use (50%+ of need situations)
Without parent prompting — the child is self-advocating
Vest accepted as part of "going out" routine
No negotiation — the tool is now integrated into identity
Outing duration extended to near-normal community participation
New environments attempted with similar success patterns
Floor drops reduced to specific high-trigger scenarios only
Not eliminated yet — but no longer the default response

When School Needs to Know: This is the moment to share the social story, break card protocol, and visual schedule with teachers and school staff. Provide laminated copies. Consistency across environments accelerates generalisation. This is also the time to introduce the same materials and protocols in NEW settings: new stores, new caregivers, school environments.

Act IV — Red Flags
These Signs Mean Get Professional Support Now.
Most families navigate floor dropping successfully with the 9-material protocol. But certain signs indicate the situation needs clinical assessment beyond a home programme. Knowing these flags is part of responsible implementation.
📞 9100 181 181 — FREE National Autism Helpline — Call Today
🔴 Sudden Onset
Floor dropping appears suddenly with no prior history. Warrants medical evaluation (pain, vestibular, neurological).
🔴 No Function Identifiable
Floor dropping occurs randomly, in all settings, with no clear trigger, across all times of day. Requires FBA by BCBA.
🔴 Worsening Despite 8 Weeks
No reduction in frequency, duration, or intensity after 8 consistent weeks of full protocol implementation. Plan needs to change.
🔴 Self-Injury During Floor Drop
Child banging head on floor, scratching, or other self-injurious behaviour during or after dropping. Requires BCBA + NeuroDev evaluation immediately.
🔴 Safety Crisis Frequency
Multiple daily floor drops in dangerous settings (parking lots, stairs, traffic). Safety management required.
🔴 Regression After Progress
Child returns to frequent floor dropping after weeks of improvement. Check: illness · sleep · major routine change · new stressor.
🔴 New Neurological Signs
Any loss of previously acquired skills accompanying floor dropping onset. Medical evaluation is urgent.

Act VI — The Close
The Questions Every Parent Asks About Floor Dropping.
Q1: How long will it take to stop the floor dropping?
Most families see significant reduction (50%+ decrease in frequency) within 8–12 weeks of consistent full-protocol implementation. Elimination of floor dropping may take 16–24 weeks depending on function complexity and consistency. Individual timelines vary.
Q2: Should I just leave my child on the floor until they get up?
"Planned ignoring" is one behavioural strategy, but it requires careful implementation. Used incorrectly (when the function is sensory, communication, or overload rather than attention), it can worsen the behaviour. A BCBA can assess whether this is appropriate for your child's specific function.
Q3: My child won't accept the weighted vest. What do I do?
Systematic desensitisation: start with 30 seconds wearing it during a highly preferred activity. Reinforce heavily. Gradually extend. If rejection persists after 4 weeks, consult your OT — compression shirts may be better tolerated than vest-style.
Q4: Can floor dropping be related to medical issues?
Yes. Hypotonia (low muscle tone), vestibular disorders, pain, and fatigue can all contribute to dropping. If floor dropping is sudden onset, associated with fatigue, or accompanied by other new symptoms — medical evaluation by a paediatrician or NeuroDev doctor is warranted.
Q5: My child is 10 and too heavy to lift. What do I do in a safety emergency?
Wrist link prevents the safety emergency before it happens. If you're in one: stay beside them on the ground, maintain safety proximity, offer regulation tools, wait. Do not attempt to lift a resistant child — injury risk to both. Exit strategy: request store staff assistance if needed.
Q6: Should we avoid outings entirely until this improves?
No. Avoidance maintains the problem. Strategic graduated exposure — starting with 10-minute outings with full protocol — builds tolerance. Total avoidance means zero practice opportunities. Plan for smaller successes, not larger avoidances.
Q7: The break card is being used too much. Is that a problem?
Initially, frequent break card use is success — it means communication is working. Over time, your BCBA will shape longer intervals between break card uses. For now, celebrate every card use as a drop prevented.
Q8: My child's school doesn't believe in these strategies. How do I get them on board?
Share this page with the school. Request a meeting with the school counsellor and resource teacher. Provide the NCAEP 2020 Evidence-Based Practices document (ncaep.fpg.unc.edu) showing these are Level I evidence-based practices. If school resistance continues, escalate to the special education coordinator.
